9.1.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what knee anatomy matters for a total knee?"
- "**Modified hinge**, tri-axial → rollback in flexion, **screw-home** in extension → a fixed hinge overloads fixation."
- "Asymmetry → tibia **3° varus**, larger medial plateau and condyle → guide cuts, rotation and tray cover."
- "**Collaterals and corners** → balancing · **PCL** (posterior cruciate ligament) → decides CR vs PS design."

### Joint type & motion
- **Synovial**, modified hinge (condyloid) → 2 tibiofemoral + 1 patellofemoral compartment
- **3 degrees of freedom** → flexion–extension (main), rotation, abduction–adduction (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 9.1 · 9.1
- Not a pure hinge → rollback + rotation → **fixed hinge** overloads fixation → salvage only
- **Medial** compartment commonest in OA (osteoarthritis) → most candidates are **varus**

#### Gait numbers
- Gait → flexion ≈70° swing, 20° stance · ab/adduction ≈10° · rotation 10–15° (Campbell)
- **Medial pivot** → posterior translation 2 mm medial vs 21 mm lateral in flexion (Campbell)
- **Screw-home** → tibia externally rotates in terminal extension, locks · **popliteus** unlocks

### Tibial surface
- **Medial plateau** → oval, larger, concave · **lateral** → round, smaller, flat to convex
- Medial condyle stays, lateral rolls back → basis of **medial-pivot** designs
- Proximal tibia normally **3° varus** to the mechanical axis (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- Medial condyle larger, more posterior → symmetrical tray leaves **posteromedial uncoverage**
[[FIG: Fig 9.2 · 9.1

#### Eminence & menisci
- True lateral film → concave medial vs convex lateral outline → read **posterior slope**
- Eminence, front → back: medial anterior root → **ACL** → lateral roots → medial posterior root → **PCL**
- Medial meniscus fixed to deep MCL and capsule · lateral mobile → medial tears commoner

### Femoral surface
- **Medial condyle** wider, more distal and posterior → compensates the 3° tibial varus
- Medial condyle carries **75%** of body weight (Handbook)
- Sagittal → small anterior, large posterior bulge = **posterior condylar offset** → deep flexion
- Offset not restored → early tibial impingement, less flexion, faster polyethylene wear
[[FIG: Fig 9.18 · 9.1

#### Groove, notch & deformity
- Anterior **trochlear groove** → skyline (Merchant) view · posterior **intercondylar notch** → tunnel view
- Valgus or rheumatoid knee → **lateral condyle hypoplasia**, distal and posterior (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 9.3 · 9.1
- Varus knee → posterior **medial** condyle more eroded
- Femoral rotation in the valgus knee → 10 Technique

### Patellar surface
- Ridges → **6 facets**: larger lateral, smaller medial, each superior, middle, inferior
- Larger lateral facet meets the higher lateral trochlear wall → resists lateral shift
- **Odd facet** → bare medial edge, touches medial condyle only beyond 120° flexion
- Ridge lies **medial** → button placed slightly medial (Prof Sherief Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 9.4 · 9.1

#### Exam extras
- Patellar cartilage → **thickest** in the body
- **Wiberg** classification → patellar shape by medial vs lateral facet size, axial view

### Extra-articular ligaments
- Four groups → **coronary**, **collaterals**, **corners** (posteromedial, posterolateral), **patellar tendon**

| Structure | Course | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Superficial MCL** (medial collateral ligament) | medial epicondyle → 7–10 cm below joint line | main valgus restraint |
| **Deep MCL** | meniscofemoral + meniscotibial (= coronary) parts | midmedial capsule |
| **POL** (posterior oblique ligament) | adductor tubercle → tibia + posterior capsule | key posteromedial corner |
| **FCL** (fibular collateral = LCL) | lateral epicondyle → fibular head, ≈70 mm | varus restraint 0–30° |
| **Popliteofibular** | popliteus tendon → fibula | ties fibula to femur |
| **Arcuate** | condensation of popliteus-origin fibres | not a separate ligament |

- Posteromedial + posterolateral **capsule** → main hyperextension restraint · cruciates minor
[[FIG: Fig 9.5 · 9.1
- Superficial MCL inserts deep to **pes anserinus** → subperiosteal release lengthens it stepwise
- Balancing → varus: medial side contracted · valgus: lateral side contracted
- **Saw injury to the MCL** → primary repair or a more constrained implant

### Intra-articular ligaments
- **Meniscofemoral** → lateral meniscus posterior horn → medial femoral condyle · variably present
- **Humphry** in front of PCL, **Wrisberg** behind → ≈22% of PCL area (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 9.6 · 9.1
- **PCL** → primary restraint to posterior tibial translation
- Lateral meniscus tied to popliteus + meniscofemoral ligament → follows condyle → fewer tears

#### Traps
- Isolated PCL tear → intact Humphry mimics an intact PCL · small drawer in internal rotation
- Sagittal MRI → dot in front of or behind PCL → mimics loose body or meniscal tear
- PS knee → PCL and these ligaments gone → only **cam and post** stop posterior sliding

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Modified hinge · tibia 3° varus · big medial condyle · ridge medial · Humphry front, Wrisberg back**

9.2.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how did knee designs evolve, and what is constraint?"
- "Resection → interposition → hinges → **total condylar (Insall 1973)** = benchmark: metal on polyethylene resurfacing."
- "Four parts → femur, tibial tray, **polyethylene insert** (the weak link), patellar button."
- "**Constraint** ↑ → stability ↑, motion ↓, fixation stress ↑ → least constraint that balances the knee."

### History
| Date | Person | Step |
|---|---|---|
| 1861 | **Ferguson** | resection arthroplasty |
| 1863 | **Verneuil** | interposition (capsule flap) |
| 19th century | **Gluck** | first prosthesis, ivory |
| 1947 | **Judet** | acrylic prostheses |
| 1950s | — | metal components |
| 1960s | **MacIntosh, McKeever** | partial tibial / patellar prostheses |
| ≈1970 | **Freeman–Swanson** (ICLH) | condylar metal-on-polyethylene resurfacing |
| 1973 | **Insall** | **total condylar** → first geometric knee |

- Lesson → resection: motion without stability · hinges: stability without durability · condylar: both
- Early fixed hinges (**Walldius**, **Shiers**) → loosening, infection · all stress at the interface
- Total condylar → survivorship 95% at 15 years, 91% at 21–23 years (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 9.7 · 9.2
- Descendants → **Insall-Burstein** PS (posterior-stabilised, 1978) and most current designs

#### Later steps
- Metal-backed trays → less polyethylene deformation and wear
- Late 1980s–1990s → patellofemoral reoperations → longer trochlea, asymmetric anterior flanges

### Standard components
| Component | Design |
|---|---|
| **Femoral** | two convex runners joined by an anterior patellar flange |
| **Tibial tray** | one-piece metal, two dished surfaces |
| **Polyethylene insert** | locks into the tray |
| **Patellar button** | polyethylene dome |

- Insert = wear part → thickness, conformity and locking decide longevity
- Polyethylene **radiolucent** → metal-to-metal gap = insert · asymmetric narrowing → wear
- Patellar resurfacing → 10 Technique

#### Sizing & slope
- Femoral sizing, increments and half sizes → 10 Technique

#### Insert slope
- **Built-in slope** → insert thicker in front · flat insert → slope cut in bone

### Constraint principle
- ↑ constraint → ↑ stability, ↓ motion → load moves from soft tissue to fixation
- Rule → **least constraint** that gives a balanced knee
- Coronal laxity on standing films → 10 Technique

#### Stepping up
- **Ultra-congruent** (deep-dish) insert → AP stability without a post → PCL lost in a CR knee
[[FIG: Fig 9.8 · 9.2
- Level chosen with **trial inserts** → step up only if unstable after balancing

### Unconstrained: resurfacing & UKA
- **Unconstrained** → native ligaments give stability → ligaments must be intact
- **Resurfacing** → joint surfaces replaced, ligaments kept, no compartment resected
- **UKA** (unicompartmental knee arthroplasty) → one condyle + its plateau
[[FIG: Fig 9.9 · 9.2
- Candidates → elderly thin, or younger as a "first" arthroplasty instead of HTO (high tibial osteotomy)

#### Selection & contraindications
- **Kozinn & Scott** (1989) → one compartment, correctable deformity, intact ACL, small contracture, good motion
- Out → inflammatory arthritis, ACL deficiency, opposite-compartment erosion
- Flexion contracture **≥15°** · arc **<90°** · varus >10°, valgus >5° (Campbell)
- Obesity → relative · only **6%** of arthroplasty patients have no contraindication (Campbell)

#### Results
- **Oxford** mobile-bearing → 94% at 10 years, 91% at 20 years (Campbell)
- Robotic fixed-bearing medial → 91.7% at 10 years · revisions: unexplained pain, loosening (Campbell)
- Fails by **aseptic loosening**, arthritis progression, proximal tibial fracture
- Registries → **more revisions** than TKA · faster recovery, more natural feel

PITFALL — UKA deformity limit
- Handbook → "deformity >5–10°" with no plane · Campbell → **>10° varus, >5° valgus** from the mechanical axis
- Say → "**UKA out if varus >10°, valgus >5°, contracture ≥15°, arc <90°**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Insall 1973 · insert = weak link · 2 mm sizes · least constraint · UKA: ACL intact, 10/5/15/90**

9.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "CR or PS — how do you choose?"
- "**CR** (cruciate-retaining) keeps the PCL → rollback, proprioception · needs a healthy, **balanced** PCL."
- "**PS** sacrifices it → **cam strikes post** → forced rollback · AP stability only, no varus–valgus."
- "Choose by PCL and patient → RA (rheumatoid arthritis), PCL loss, patellectomy, big deformity → **PS**."

### Cruciate-retaining (CR)
- Keeps the **PCL** → AP stability, femoral **rollback**, quadriceps efficiency
[[FIG: Fig 9.10 · 9.3
- Normal flexion → **rolling + gliding**, contact moves back (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 9.11 · 9.3
- No PCL in deep flexion → femur rolls off the back → **impingement** → failure
- Tight PCL → stress each flexion → **lift-off** (seesaw) → loosening

#### Balancing the PCL
- Tight or loose PCL, recession, conversion → 11 Balancing

#### Keep it or not
- Pro → native PCL replicates anatomy · con → degenerate PCL may rupture later (Prof Shokry)
- Egypt → late presentation → PCL health doubtful → late rupture fails the whole knee

### Posterior-stabilised (PS)
- PCL sacrificed → **cam engages post** → forced rollback
[[FIG: Fig 9.12 · 9.3
- Post resists posterior translation only → collaterals keep coronal stability → no answer to absent MCL
- Usual choice → PCL absent or deficient, released for big deformity, after **patellectomy**
- Most surgeons → **PS**: CR balancing much harder → early career (Prof Abd Elkarim)

#### Lecturer's policy
- Prof Shokry → sacrifices it in all → late patients, poor soft tissues
- Box cut removes extra femoral bone → matters at revision

### PS vs CR — key differences
| Feature | PS | CR |
|---|---|---|
| **Cam–post** | cam strikes post → rollback | none |
| **Insert** | conforming (dished) | flatter → allows rollback |
| **Indication** | RA, PCL injury | intact PCL, no RA |
| **X-ray** | box, larger femoral cut | normal pegs |
| **Proprioception** | inferior | superior (native PCL) |
| **Flexion** | ≈120° | 105–110° |
| **Wear** | lower, load spread | higher, point contact |
| **Late failure** | post wear, cam jump | late PCL rupture → instability |

- Table rows and flexion numbers → Handbook sheet (Handbook)
- Evidence → ≈4° difference favouring CR, maybe not significant (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- PCL policy = surgeon's philosophy → both correct
- Fluoroscopy → **paradoxical anterior sliding** in many CR knees → rollback less reliable

#### Practical points
- Earlier flat CR inserts → high contact stress → wear · newer ones more conforming
[[FIG: Fig 9.13 · 9.3
- Slope by design → 10 Technique
- Posterior sag or drawer years after CR → **late PCL insufficiency**

### Complications of PS & CR
- **Cam jump** → loose flexion gap, deep flexion ± varus–valgus stress → cam slips over the post
- Prevent → balance the flexion gap · treat → revision
- **Post wear**, breakage → femoral component hits the post in hyperextension
[[FIG: Fig 9.14 · 9.3
- Post impingement ↑ → flexed femoral component, more slope, hyperextension

#### Survival & clunk
- **Mayo Clinic** → 15-year survival PS 77% (2728 knees) vs CR 90% (5389) (Campbell)
- **Patellar clunk** → nodule at quadriceps tendon–superior pole catches in the box
- Clunk at **30–45°** flexion on active extension (Campbell) → usually arthroscopic excision
- Causes → proximal button overhang · box starts below trochlea · longer trochlea → rarer

#### CR wear
- CR insert less conforming → higher contact stress → faster wear
- Tight PCL → condyles ride the posterior polyethylene lip → extreme stress

PITFALL — which design wears more and fails late?
- Handbook files wear and PCL failure under PS complications → both belong to **CR**
- Say → "**CR: flat insert wears more, PCL may rupture late · PS: post wear, cam jump, clunk**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **CR = balanced PCL, slope in bone · PS = cam–post, slope in insert, box · clunk at 30–45°**

9.4.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when do you need more constraint?"
- "**CCK** = PS with a tall, wide post in a deep box → varus–valgus control → weak but present collaterals."
- "**Rotating hinge** → linked, rotation free → global ligament loss, collateral bone loss, tumour, salvage."
- "Constraint replaces **absent** ligaments, never tight ones → those are released · more constraint → stems."

### Constrained designs — overview
- **Constrained** → AP + varus–valgus stability → deficient collaterals or massive bone loss
- Mainly → **revision**, valgus with incompetent MCL, neuropathic or post-traumatic knee
- More constraint → more load on fixation → **stems** share it
- Some systems → stemmed femur only in revision sets · primary: stemmed tibia only (Prof Sherief Khaled)

### Non-hinged constrained condylar knee (CCK)
- **CCK** (constrained condylar knee) = modified PS → larger post, deeper box
[[FIG: Fig 9.15 · 9.4
- Post against box walls → varus–valgus control, small toggle · otherwise acts as PS
- Post + fixation take ligament loads → needs **weak but present** collaterals
- X-ray → PS look-alike, deeper box, taller wider post, usually **stems**

#### Use & results
- Revision with instability · primary with extreme valgus + **MCL** insufficiency
- Stems → cemented or modular press-fit · mobile-bearing option → ↓ tibial forces
- Cannot block **recurvatum** · loosening feared in the young
- Primary CCK → revision 0.8%, 10-year survival 97.6% (Campbell)

### Hinged (linked) prostheses
- Linked by a **hinge** → blocks recurvatum
- Fixed hinges failed → no rotation → torque into bone · rotating bearing dissipates it
[[FIG: Fig 9.16 · 9.4

| Design | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Endo-model** | femoral bush between condyles + tibial stem |
| **Kinematic / Noiles** | femoral axle rotates in a tibial sleeve |
| **S-ROM** | axle rotates in a stemmed polyethylene insert |
| **NexGen rotating hinge** | posterior axle → tibial stem: flexion, extension, rotation |

- **Kinematic Rotating Hinge** → 2 polyethylene + CoCr bearings → flexion–extension + axial rotation
- Locked sagittal and coronal, free axial rotation → ↓ interface force

#### Indications
- **Global ligament deficiency**, bone loss at collateral origins, distal femoral tumour resection
- Elderly distal femoral nonunion or periprosthetic fracture · hyperextension instability · gap mismatch
- **Neuromuscular disease**, limb salvage · **Charcot** knee → rotating hinge + brace
- Primary → only if the flexion gap may "jump" a CCK → worse outcomes

#### Results
- Early Kinematic hinge no better than **GUEPAR** · **S-ROM** → far fewer complications
- Complications → **infection**, loosening, extensor mechanism problems, hinge failure

### Compartment coverage
| Class | Replaced |
|---|---|

#### Patellofemoral arthroplasty (PFA)
- Isolated PF arthritis, often trochlear dysplasia · ideal <65 years, minimal coronal deformity

- Mobile theory → lower contact stress, rotation in gait, self-aligns small tray malrotation

#### Technique traps
- Insert follows the **femur** → tray, insert, femur set together on a diathermy mark
- Tibia rotated unlike femur → insert sits **15°** off → prominent → arthrofibrosis

- **LCS** (low contact stress) → tibial cut as rotation reference → needs a well-balanced knee

#### Complications & evidence
- **Spin-out** (rotational dislocation) → unbalanced gaps · plus **backside wear**
- Spun-out → open reduction + thicker insert, or revision if gaps unbalanced
- Evidence → more short- and midterm revisions · one meta-analysis no difference
